name: 510(k), De Novo and PMA for AI Devices
blurb: Which FDA pathway an AI device takes, and why most use 510(k).
title: 510(k), De Novo and PMA for AI Devices
answer: Most AI devices are moderate risk and are cleared through the 510(k) pathway as substantially equivalent to an existing predicate. Novel moderate risk devices without a predicate use De Novo, which then creates a predicate for followers, and high risk devices need premarket approval with clinical evidence.

reading.body:
Most AI medical devices are moderate risk and reach the market through 510(k) clearance against an existing predicate, not through De Novo or PMA.

The pathway follows risk, not novelty. A device that is substantially equivalent to something already cleared can cite that predicate and avoid new clinical evidence. A novel moderate risk device has no predicate to cite, so it takes De Novo, which is slower and costlier but leaves the applicant owning the predicate that later products must cite. High risk devices go to premarket approval and carry a clinical evidence requirement.

The De Novo step is where the regulatory structure compounds. Each successful De Novo converts a one-off review into an asset, because the cleared device becomes the comparison point for followers. That shapes which AI products get built and in what order, since a company choosing between a fast 510(k) on a known device type and a slower De Novo on a new one is choosing between speed and control of a category.

The data covers the three pathways and the logic connecting them. It does not give counts by pathway, clearance times, or fees, and it does not say how any specific device was classified. The npj Digital Medicine finding is stated as a general pattern, not a breakdown. Nothing here ties these pathways to compute, data centers, or power, and the regulatory constraint described is evidentiary rather than physical.
